book: 192 - Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_

chapters.file: ch25 - 14. Who Watches the Justice League.md
chapters.relation: Judges the two heroes by negative consequentialism (attributed to Hume and Popper): the better hero is the one who best prevents future suffering, including suffering he might cause himself. Superman qualifies because he hands the League—Batman above all—the means to defeat him (as in Injustice) and kills himself with gold kryptonite after executing Mr. Mxyzptlk in 'What Happened to the Man of Tomorrow?', while Hume's reason-is-slave-of-the-passions reading explains the Zod neck-snap in Man of Steel as passion-driven necessity. Batman's countermeasures in 'Tower of Babel' and Justice League: Doom stop every Leaguer except Batman himself ('My failsafe is the Justice League'), an arrogance that loses him this round.

A scripted Lois Lane–Batman interview argues that the Batmobile/Batwing upgrade cycle and Wayne Enterprises' multinational production enact Marx's 'metabolic rift' (via John Bellamy Foster): both take from nature and return unprocessable waste faster than the planet can replenish, so protecting Gotham's way of life perpetuates an infinite environmental crisis of consumption. Solar-powered Superman wins the environmental showdown on lifestyle impact, but Batman counters that Krypton's ecological suicide makes Superman an 'environmental refugee,' not a model. The chapter's real verdict is Bruce's line 'We are all Bruce Wayne': human consumers must rebalance the human–nature relationship before finite resources like fresh water run out.

Starting from the Joker's 'You made me' / Batman's 'You made me first' exchange in Tim Burton's Batman, the chapter argues origin stories fix character: Bruce's witnessed trauma destines him to darkness (and we expect his death to match), while Kal-El is sent to Earth as an act of hope that the chapter reads through William James's will-to-believe—belief itself makes success possible, like Bruce's ropeless leap in The Dark Knight Rises. Against 'I can do whatever I want' free will it deploys Schopenhauer's 'we can do what we will, but we cannot will what we will': Bruce cannot will away his vengeance, and Red Son's Soviet-raised Superman shows biology and upbringing determining who Clark becomes. Superman still wins because his origin story permits the hope that Bruce's cannot.

chapters.file: ch28 - Round Four Decision—Batman! It’s Always Darkest Before the Knight.md
ch29 - 17. Batman’s Mask in Aristotle’s Drama.md
chapters.relation: Reads Batman's defining difference—the mask—through Aristotle's Poetics: Batman is mimesis, a theatrical performance (the prosopon) engineered to produce pity, fear, and suspense, while unmasked, transparent Superman is the more Platonic figure who wants the Mirror of Truth in All-Star Superman to confirm Clark Kent is his real self. Batman's acting literally beats Superman in The Dark Knight Returns, where the fight is won by a staged death from a fake-heart pill, and his 'Feat of Clay' interrogation shows him performing cruelty to weaponize criminals' imaginations. Because the role is imitable—Robin, Batman Incorporated, the Sons of Batman—'Batman is an idea' anyone can become, whereas Eco's 'Myth of Superman' explains why the unimitatable alien preserves rather than changes his world.

Borrowing Harry Frankfurt's move of philosophically defining a colloquial term (as Frankfurt did for 'bullshit'), it defines a 'dick' as someone who willfully disregards others' needs and argues Superman is one: the vending-machine thought experiment shows he could rescue a sinking school bus in less time than it takes Clark to buy a chocolate bar, so saving people at little or no cost to himself is obligatory, not supererogatory. Peter Singer's famine-and-affluence argument extends the same obligation to the affluent reader, while the SuperBat arc of Superman/Batman #53–56—in which Batman temporarily gains Superman's powers and empties every city's jails in one night—proves Superman could do vastly more than he does. Batman, who risks his mortal life and seeks out strangers to save, is 'not a dick' and wins the round.

A game designer explains why roughly a hundred Batman games include acclaimed ones while no good Superman game exists: flow (Csikszentmihaly's balance of challenge and skill) is impossible with a hero who is either omnipotent or wholesale nullified by kryptonite, whereas Batman's trainable skills and acquirable, losable equipment—like Samus Aran's suit in Metroid—give designers levers for escalation, and the player can even supply the detective's brain. Superman's 'heart,' the willpower that unleashes his full might (as in Saint Seiya's unadaptable Cosmo), cannot be tested through a controller. Playing journalist Clark Kent's investigations and no-win dilemmas is sketched as the one route to a decent Superman game.

Argues Batman is more heroic than Superman because heroism requires supererogation and replicability: Wesley Autrey's subway rescue, done without obligation, outranks Sullenberger's 'just what we're trained for,' and unlike otherworldly Superman, Batman's human abilities let the rest of us imagine imitating him—heroism begets heroism, as Gordon's coat around young Bruce's shoulders helped make Batman. Batman is framed as the answer to the problem of evil in Susan Neiman's secular form: Rachel Dawes' challenge that good people do something, on the Rousseau side of the Enlightenment debate that morality must make evil intelligible (against Voltaire's refusal). Superman's overwhelming power makes relying on reason superfluous, so he becomes a symbol of what we can't be, while the Dark Knight models what we can.

Argues that Christian Bale's Batman, not the alien Superman, embodies Nietzsche's Übermensch: a mortal, flawed, lonely hero whose identity is forged in the unreconciled struggle between Dionysian vengeance and Apollonian reason across Nolan's trilogy. Batman Begins enacts eternal recurrence as Bruce repeatedly relives and integrates the well, the opera, and his parents' murder; The Dark Knight's Joker is Batman's Janus-faced shadow whose ferry experiment nearly proves the herd's 'gravity of madness,' and Dent's fall shows what Batman resists becoming. Superman II's temporarily mortal Superman is beaten by a truck driver and retreats to invincibility, proving the immortal alien can never overreach mortal limits as the Übermensch must.

chapters.file: ch34 - Post-Fight Analysis Superhero Truthers Speak Out!.md
ch35 - 22. Unmasking the World and Its Heroes.md
chapters.relation: Claims the Superman-vs-Batman debate misses the point: both heroes are cave-escapers who must first see beyond appearances—Bruce renouncing vengeance on Joe Chill and then shaking Gotham from apathy (the ferries refusing the Joker's detonators), Clark learning from Jonathan and Jor-El that his powers are not for touchdowns but to lead humanity out by example. Masks serve the Socratic warning of the Apology that the just man must act privately to survive—Jonathan Kent dies keeping Clark's secret—yet risk becoming their own trap, from Smallville's Red Kryptonite ring to Batman's sonar surveillance that Lucius Fox calls too much power for one person. The chapter closes on Socratic ignorance and Man of Steel's genesis chambers: a hero, like Socrates, knows his wisdom is worth nothing, and anyone who chooses can be one.

chapters.file: ch36 - 23. I Fight Crime in My Sleep.md
chapters.relation: A Fight Club-style Arkham case study: a patient's hallucinated Superman companion is diagnosed by a Buddhist psychiatrist who explains the three marks of existence—impermanence, non-self, and dissatisfaction—arguing superheroes impose order and a fabricated second self on a world that resists both, so Superman's super-intellect and even flight are distractions (levitation should be ignored; the Buddha-eye beats x-ray vision) while Batman's violence and psychosis, compared to American Psycho's Patrick Bateman, make awakening impossible—both are victims of Mara. A robber literally named David Hume objects that the heroes' law and order is grounded on what ought to be rather than what is, and a Gandhi quote on preferring one's own bad government explains why Batman finally kryptonites his alien 'friend.' The verdict inverts the book's debate: conquering the deceiver within is the only superpower worth having.

Written in the Joker's voice, it plays the fifty-third card no other contributor considered: maybe both 'heroes' are the villains—Superman's public saves are attention-seeking ego when he could help unseen, and Batman selfishly pours billions into Bat-toys instead of donating it to save millions of dying children. Its deeper target is our hypocrisy: the Dark Knight ferry scene is unbelievable because in reality we would climb over each other to push the button, since we are only as moral as our circumstances allow while buying sweatshop chocolate and bacon and calling ourselves good. The genuine 'super-man' would drop the pretense of morality altogether, live by his own lights before dancing with the devil, and laugh as the world burns.

holes.name: The Metabolic Rift
holes.what: Marx's ecological idea, revived by John Bellamy Foster, that capitalist production ruptures the nutrient exchange between society and nature, accumulating waste faster than ecosystems can process it.
holes.why: Chapter 26's entire Lois Lane–Batman dialogue charges the Bat-gear upgrade cycle and Wayne Enterprises with generating metabolic rifts of infinite consumption and waste.

holes.name: Mimesis and Catharsis (Poetics)
holes.what: Aristotle's account of drama as imitation (mimesis) of human action that arouses pity and fear (catharsis) in an audience.
holes.why: Chapter 29 defines Batman as mimesis—a theatrical mask whose staged death defeats Superman in The Dark Knight Returns—and taxonomy has no Poetics concept to map this to.

holes.name: Umberto Eco
holes.what: Italian semiotician and novelist whose essay 'The Myth of Superman' argues comic-book commerce demands formulaic plots that keep Superman's world permanently unchanged.
holes.why: Chapter 29 uses Eco's thesis to explain why Superman preserves the status quo while Batman actively tries to remake Gotham and can be imitated by successors.

holes.name: Flow (optimal experience)
holes.what: Mihaly Csikszentmihaly's state of deep engagement that occurs when a challenge exactly matches a person's skill, between boredom and anxiety.
holes.why: Chapter 31 explains the absence of a good Superman video game through flow: an invincible hero can never be matched to player skill, unlike equipment-driven, trainable Batman.

holes.name: Supererogation (beyond the call of duty)
holes.what: Acts that are morally admirable but beyond obligation—good to perform though not wrong to omit.
holes.why: Chapter 32 builds its thesis that Batman is the more heroic on supererogation as the mark of heroism: Autrey's unobligated subway rescue is heroic, Sullenberger's trained duty is not, and Superman's near-obligatory guarding of Earth falls short.
